title: The inner light
hook: George Fox and the Quakers: there is that of God in everyone, found in silent waiting

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was practice of the presence: Brother Lawrence and his omelet. Your line was God among the pots. Which chore did you do with God in the room? Day two hundred seventy-nine.

Imagine walking into a plain room with wooden benches facing each other. No altar, no pulpit, no music. People come in and sit down. And then nothing happens. Nobody leads. Nobody speaks. Five minutes. Twenty. The only sounds are a cough, a creaking bench, a bird outside. And then, maybe, someone stands, says a few quiet sentences, and sits down again. Then more silence. For many Quakers, that is what worship looks like, and has for more than three hundred and fifty years. It began with a restless young man in England. Today: the inner light.

George Fox was born in 1624, in a time of civil war and religious turmoil in England. As a young man he was desperate for spiritual answers. He went from minister to minister, and none of them could help him. And then, he wrote in his Journal, when all his hopes in people were gone, he heard a voice that said, in his own old English: "There is one, even Christ Jesus, that can speak to thy condition." His heart, he says, leapt for joy. Fox came to believe that God speaks directly to every person, not only through clergy or buildings. He pointed to the Gospel of John, which says of Christ: "That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world." Every man, every person. Friends came to call this the inner light, or the light within. So Fox's followers, who called themselves Friends, and whom others nicknamed Quakers, would gather in silence and wait for that light to speak. In a letter from prison in 1656, Fox urged them to "walk cheerfully over the world, answering that of God in every one." That of God in every one. Not only in the people who agree with you. In the jailer. In the stranger. In the enemy. That conviction pushed many Friends into costly action over the centuries: early work against slavery, prison reform, refusing to fight in wars. Today there are different kinds of Quaker worship. Many meetings still wait in silence. Others, especially in Africa and the Americas, have pastors, hymns and sermons. But the conviction runs through all of them: there is something of God in everyone.
screen: `SPEAK TO THY CONDITION.` · `THE TRUE LIGHT, WHICH LIGHTETH EVERY MAN.` · `SILENT WAITING.` · `THAT OF GOD IN EVERY ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in silence, and if you can, with one other person. If someone is near, ask them to sit quietly with you for two minutes. No talking, no phones. If you're alone, picture someone you know sitting across from you. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to make anything happen. Just wait. If a thought feels like light, hold it. If it's only noise, let it pass. The bell holds the time.
The inner light. The Quaker conviction that God's light shines within every person, found by waiting in silence.
Your line: that of God in everyone. Today, with one person who annoys you, look for it. Just look. Day two hundred seventy-nine.
